name: Anguidae
commonName: Slow Worms, Glass Lizards & Alligator Lizards

children.name: Anguinae
children.description: The Old World and North American legless or near-legless anguid lizards, including slow worms, European glass lizards, and Asian glass lizards.

children.name: Anguis
children.description: Slow worms of Europe and southwestern Asia. These smooth-scaled, copper-toned legless lizards are distinguished from snakes by their eyelids, external ear openings, and autotomous tails. They are fossorial and secretive, foraging on slugs, earthworms, and small invertebrates.

children.name: Anguis fragilis
children.description: The common slow worm (Anguis fragilis) is a non-venomous species of legless lizard native to Europe.

children.name: Anguis colchica
children.description: Anguis colchica, the eastern slow worm, is a species of legless lizard in the family Anguidae found in eastern and northern Europe and Asia.

children.name: Anguis graeca
children.description: Anguis graeca, the Greek slow worm, is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae found in Greece, Albania, and North Macedonia.

children.name: Anguis cephallonica
children.description: Anguis cephallonica, the Peloponnese slow worm, is a species of legless lizard in the family Anguidae endemic to Greece. It is found in the Peloponnese and islands of Cephalonia, Ithaca, and Zakynthos in the Ionian Sea, at elevations of up to 1,340 m. Its natural habitats are temperate forests, temperate shrubland, Mediterranean-type shrubby vegetation, temperate grassland, arable land, pastureland, plantations, and rural gardens. The species can be distinguished from all other slow worms by the greater number of scale rows around the body and the distinctive color pattern on its side. Peloponnese slow worms give birth to live litters of 3–26 young. They are listed as being a species of least concern on the IUCN Red List.

children.name: Anguis veronensis
children.description: Anguis veronensis, commonly known as the Italian slow worm, is a European lizard species in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Anguis bilineata
children.description: Distributed across the Iberian Peninsula and southern France, characterised by two pale lateral stripes on the dorsum. It prefers cooler, moister habitats such as scrub, heathland, and humid forest edges. Genetic data confirm deep divergence from the northern A. fragilis clade.

children.name: Pseudopus
children.description: Large, near-legless lizards of Europe and central Asia, bearing tiny vestigial hind-limb flaps near the cloaca. Formerly placed in Ophisaurus, Pseudopus apodus is one of the largest lizards on the European continent.

children.name: Pseudopus apodus
children.description: The sheltopusik, also spelled scheltopusik, sheltopusick, scheltopusick, sheltopusic, or scheltopusic (Pseudopus apodus), and also commonly known as Pallas's glass lizard, the European legless lizard, or the European glass lizard, is a species of large glass lizard found from Southern Europe to Central Asia.

children.name: Ophisaurus
children.description: North American glass lizards — slender, limbless or nearly limbless lizards whose tails shatter along fracture planes when seized by predators, giving the group its common name. They inhabit open pine flatwoods, grasslands, and damp meadows.

children.name: Ophisaurus ventralis
children.description: The eastern glass lizard (Ophisaurus ventralis) is a species of legless lizard in the family Anguidae and the longest and heaviest species of glass lizards in the genus Ophisaurus, endemic to the Southeastern United States. The streamlined, legless species is often confused with snakes. Glass lizards differ from snakes as they possess a moveable eyelid and an external ear opening as well as a lateral groove that separates the different types of scales on the animal, while all three of these features are absent in snakes. Snakes also have flexible jaws while lizards do not. Ventralis comes from the Latin "venter" meaning belly; this is in reference to the snake-like movement.

children.name: Ophisaurus attenuatus
children.description: The slender glass lizard (Ophisaurus attenuatus) is a legless lizard in the glass lizard subfamily (Anguinae).

children.name: Ophisaurus compressus
children.description: The island glass lizard (Ophisaurus compressus) is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae. The species is endemic to the southeastern United States.

children.name: Ophisaurus mimicus
children.description: The mimic glass lizard (Ophisaurus mimicus) is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae. The species is endemic to the Southeastern United States. The mimic glass lizard is dark brown to black with a dark middorsal stripe down the body and on most of the tail. They have 3-4 dark stripes separated by pale stripes above the lateral grooves. They have a very distinct anatomy of the axis specifically when it comes to their second vertebra which could be attributed to an ecological adaptation, feeding, and/or defensive behavior that requires high head and neck mobility.

children.name: Dopasia
children.description: Asian glass lizards of South and Southeast Asia; formerly included within Ophisaurus. These slender, legless or near-legless lizards inhabit forest edges, grasslands, and agricultural margins across a wide band from India to Indonesia.

children.name: Dopasia gracilis
children.description: Dopasia gracilis, known commonly as the Asian glass lizard, the Burmese glass lizard, or the Indian glass snake, is a species of legless lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Dopasia harti
children.description: Dopasia harti, also known commonly as the Chinese glass lizard and Hart's glass lizard, is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae. The species is native to south-eastern Asia.

children.name: Dopasia sokolovi
children.description: Dopasia sokolovi, Sokolov's glass lizard, is a species of lizard of the Anguidae family. It is found in Vietnam.

children.name: Dopasia buettikoferi
children.description: Dopasia buettikoferi, also known commonly as the Bornean glass snake and Buettikofer's glass lizard, is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae. The species is native to Indonesia and Malaysia on the island of Borneo.

children.name: Dopasia ludovici
children.description: Dopasia ludovici, also known commonly as Ludovic's glass lizard, is a species of lizard in the subfamily Anguinae of the family Anguidae. The species is native to Southeast Asia.

children.name: Diploglossinae
children.description: Caribbean and Central American anguid lizards, predominantly limbed or partially limbed, inhabiting forests and rocky outcrops across the West Indies and adjacent mainland.

children.name: Diploglossus
children.description: Galliwasp lizards of the Caribbean islands and Central America; stout-bodied, short-limbed, secretive lizards that live in leaf litter and under rocks. Several species are threatened by habitat loss and invasive predators.

children.name: Diploglossus monotropis
children.description: Diploglossus monotropis is a species of lizard of the Diploglossidae family.

children.name: Diploglossus pleei
children.description: Endemic to Martinique in the Lesser Antilles; a medium-sized galliwasp of forested hillsides and boulder-strewn ravines. Seriously threatened by habitat loss and introduced mongooses and rats. Named after the French naturalist and physician Auguste Plée.

children.name: Diploglossus lessonae
children.description: The Brazilian galliwasp (Diploglossus lessonae) is a carnivorous species of lizard in the family Diploglossidae.

children.name: Diploglossus fasciatus
children.description: Diploglossus fasciatus, the banded galliwasp, is a species of lizard of the family Diploglossidae.

children.name: Diploglossus costatus
children.description: One of the mainland Central American galliwasps, recorded from Costa Rica and Panama in humid lowland forest. Adults are medium-sized with smooth, brown dorsal scales and pale undersides. Its secretive habits mean encounters are rare despite a presumably broad range.

children.name: Diploglossus millepunctatus
children.description: The dotted galliwasp or Malpelo galliwasp (Diploglossus millepunctatus) is a carnivorous species of lizard endemic to Malpelo Island, Colombia.

children.name: Diploglossus nigropunctatus
children.description: Diploglossus nigropunctatus, the Cuban spotted galliwasp, is a species of lizard of the Diploglossidae family endemic to Cuba.

children.name: Diploglossus obscurus
children.description: Previously considered extinct and rediscovered on La Désirade islet off Guadeloupe in the 1990s; now a conservation priority. Its plain, dark-brown coloration makes it difficult to spot among leaf litter. Habitat destruction and introduced predators remain the principal threats.

children.name: Diploglossus warreni
children.description: Caribicus warreni, commonly known as the Haitian giant galliwasp or the Hispaniolan giant galliwasp, is a species of lizard in the family Diploglossidae.

children.name: Diploglossus butleri
children.description: Recorded from Jamaica; a relatively little-known galliwasp named in honour of the naturalist Arthur Butler. It inhabits moist montane forest at higher elevations than most Jamaican congeners. Little field data exist on its diet or reproductive biology.

children.name: Celestus
children.description: A diverse genus of Caribbean galliwasps with limbs better developed than in Diploglossus; found throughout the Greater and Lesser Antilles. Several species are island endemics of conservation concern.

children.name: Celestus occiduus
children.description:
The Jamaican giant galliwasp or sinking galliwasp (Celestus occiduus) is a possibly extinct species of lizard in the Diploglossidae. It was endemic to Jamaica. It was last recorded in mid-19th century. Its population was ravaged and likely exterminated by introduced predators like mongooses. Recent surveys, while extensive, have not yet been exhaustive, given the difficulties of access into and around the Black River Morass, leaving room for some hope that the species may persist.
The Jamaican galliwasp was the largest anguid skink on the island with a head-body length of 32 cms. Early observers noted that lived in holes near swamps and fed on crabs but it more likely lived among rocks and fed on insects. The last record of the species was in 1840. The lizard was stout and the forelimb was a third longer than the head. The tail was laterally compressed and the light brown body had about fifteen cross bands. Around 30 specimens are known in collections around the world.

children.name: Celestus enneagrammus
children.description: Siderolamprus enneagrammus, the Huaxteca lesser galliwasp, is a species of lizard of the Diploglossidae family.

children.name: Celestus barbouri
children.description: Celestus barbouri, also known commonly as Barbour's galliwasp and the limestone forest galliwasp, is a species of lizard in the family Diploglossidae.

children.name: Celestus crusculus
children.description: thumb | right | Geographic distribution of Celestus crusculus (Native to Jamaica) Celestus crusculus, the Jamaican galliwasp or Garman's galliwasp, is a species of lizard of the Diploglossidae family.

children.name: Celestus curtissi
children.description: Panolopus curtissi, also known commonly as Curtiss' galliwasp, Curtis's galliwasp, and the Hispaniolan khaki galliwasp, is a species of lizard in the family Diploglossidae endemic to the island of Hispaniola and surrounding islets.

children.name: Celestus stenurus
children.description: Comptus stenurus, the Hispaniolan keeled galliwasp or Cope's galliwasp, is a species of lizard of the Diploglossidae family endemic to the Caribbean island of Hispaniola (in both the Dominican Republic and Haiti).

children.name: Celestus warreni
children.description: Caribicus warreni, commonly known as the Haitian giant galliwasp or the Hispaniolan giant galliwasp, is a species of lizard in the family Diploglossidae.

children.name: Celestus ateles
children.description: Endemic to Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands; a small, secretive galliwasp of moist limestone forest and ravines. Its small limbs are functional but rarely used for rapid locomotion; it tends to wriggle rather than run. Endangered by habitat conversion and invasive predators.

children.name: Celestus costatus
children.description: Panolopus costatus, the Hispaniolan smooth galliwasp or common Hispaniolan galliwasp, is a species of lizard of the Diploglossidae family.

children.name: Celestus fowleri
children.description: Celestus fowleri, also known commonly as the bromeliad galliwasp and Fowler's galliwasp, is a species of lizard in the family Diploglossidae.

children.name: Celestus intermedius
children.description: Occurs in Cuba's eastern provinces; morphologically intermediate between several Cuban Celestus species, hence its name. Found in both dry scrub and the edges of humid forest. A diurnal forager, it is active in warm weather and retreats underground during cooler months.

children.name: Celestus macrotus
children.description: Celestus macrotus, La Selle galliwasp or Thomas's galliwasp, is a species of lizard of the family Diploglossidae.

children.name: Celestus xerampelinus
children.description: Known from Hispaniola; its name refers to the reddish-brown, dried-vine coloration of adults. It is a forest-floor species that relies on leaf litter and fallen wood for shelter and foraging. Probably viviparous, as is typical for galliwasps.

children.name: Celestus dunni
children.description: Described from Panama and Costa Rica; named for Emmett Reid Dunn, a prolific herpetologist of Central American fauna. A medium-sized galliwasp of humid lowland and premontane forest. Its mainland distribution sets it apart from the largely Caribbean Celestus radiation.

children.name: Wetmorena
children.description: A monotypic genus of anguid lizard endemic to Hispaniola, named after the ornithologist Alexander Wetmore. Closely related to Celestus and Diploglossus, it is one of the rarer and less-studied Caribbean galliwasps.

children.name: Wetmorena haetiana
children.description: Wetmorena haetiana, the Hispaniolan earless galliwasp or earless galliwasp, is an endangered species of lizard of the Diploglossidae family endemic to the Caribbean island of Hispaniola (in the Dominican Republic and Haiti).

children.name: Sauresia
children.description: A small genus of diminutive Caribbean anguid lizards from Hispaniola, closely related to Celestus. These tiny, poorly known lizards inhabit leaf litter in humid forests.

children.name: Sauresia sexlineata
children.description: The best-known member of Sauresia; found in Hispaniola's lowland and foothill forests where it shelters in leaf litter. Distinguished by six pale dorsal lines on a brown ground colour. Poorly studied, but viviparous reproduction is presumed based on close relatives.

children.name: Sauresia lineata
children.description: A second, smaller Hispaniolan Sauresia; similar in appearance but differing in scale counts and proportions. Like its congener it is a leaf-litter specialist of humid forest. Its population status is largely unknown; surveys are hampered by its cryptic habits.

children.name: Gerrhonotinae
children.description: The alligator lizards of North and Central America; limbed, keeled-scaled lizards named for their rough, 'armoured' appearance. They range from coniferous forests of western Canada to cloud forests of Central America.

children.name: Elgaria
children.description: Western North American alligator lizards; agile, keeled-scaled predators of rocky slopes, oak woodland, and chaparral from British Columbia to Mexico. They defend themselves vigorously with biting and tail autotomy.

children.name: Elgaria multicarinata
children.description: The southern alligator lizard (Elgaria multicarinata) is a common species of lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Elgaria coeruleus
children.description: Ranges from British Columbia through the Pacific Northwest and Sierra Nevada; tolerates cooler temperatures than most lizards, remaining active even at low ambient temperatures. Its dorsum is brown to olive with irregular dark crossbands. Viviparous; gives birth to 2–15 live young in late summer.

children.name: Elgaria kingii
children.description: The Madrean alligator lizard (Elgaria kingii), also known commonly as King's alligator lizard and el lagarto de montaña in Mexican Spanish, is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae. The species is native to the southwestern United States and adjacent northwestern Mexico.

children.name: Elgaria panamintina
children.description: The Panamint alligator lizard (Elgaria panamintina) is a species of lizard in the Anguidae family.

children.name: Elgaria coerulea shastensis
children.description: Sometimes treated as a full species, restricted to the Shasta County region of northern California. Distinguished from nearby E. coeruleus populations by colour pattern and scale count differences. Inhabits rocky forest edges and streamsides in montane terrain.

children.name: Elgaria velazquezi
children.description: The central peninsular alligator lizard (Elgaria velazquezi) is a species of medium-sized lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Abronia
children.description: Arboreal alligator lizards of Mexico and Central America; largely tree-dwelling, with prehensile tails adapted for life in cloud forest bromeliads and mossy branches. Over 30 species are known, many described in the past two decades.

children.name: Abronia graminea
children.description:
The Mexican alligator lizard (Abronia graminea), also known as the green arboreal alligator lizard, is an endangered species of lizard endemic to the Sierra Madre de Oaxaca highlands of Mexico. It can be found in the states of Puebla, Veracruz, and Oaxaca. It was originally described under the genus Gerrhonotus as Gerrhonotus gramineus by Edward D. Cope in 1864.
The Mexican alligator lizard adopts an arboreal lifestyle and is commonly found inhabiting the bromeliads among mesic cloud or pine-oak forest canopies. This habitat offers a humid temperate climate with summer rains. The preferred diet of this species is a variety of insects. Colour patterns of the Mexican alligator lizard can range from bright emerald green to dark teal blue; juvenile colouration is a tan ground colour with dark crossbands.

children.name: Abronia taeniata
children.description: Abronia taeniata, the banded arboreal alligator lizard or bromeliad arboreal alligator lizard, is a vulnerable species of arboreal alligator lizard described in 1828 by Arend Friedrich August Wiegmann.

children.name: Abronia campbelli
children.description: Abronia campbelli, commonly known as Campbell's alligator lizard, is species of critically endangered arboreal alligator lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Abronia fimbriata
children.description: Abronia fimbriata is a species of lizard endemic to the mountains of east-central Guatemala, including Sierra de Xucaneb, Sierra de las Minas, Sierra de Chuacús and Sierra de los Cuchumatanes, and is found in the cloud forests at elevations of 1,400–2,100 m.

children.name: Abronia mixteca
children.description: Abronia mixteca , the Mixtecan arboreal alligator lizard, is a vulnerable species of arboreal alligator lizards described in 1967 by Charles Mitchill Bogert and Ann Porter.

children.name: Abronia matudai
children.description: Abronia matudai, also known commonly as Matuda's arboreal alligator lizard and escorpión arborícola de Matuda in New World Spanish, is a species of endangered arboreal alligator lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Abronia vasconcelosii
children.description: Abronia vasconcelosii, sometimes known as Bocourt's arboreal alligator lizard, is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Abronia aurita
children.description: Cope's arboreal alligator lizard (Abronia aurita) is a species of lizard found in two isolated locations in Guatemala, one in the Alta Verapaz Department and one in the Jalapa Department. These lizard are found only in high altitudes of 2,000 to 2,600 feet above sea level, on the west and south sides of the mountain ranges. This lizard is one of 28 species of alligator lizards, most being arboreal, meaning they live in trees. These omnivores are considered endangered because of their small population size and they face extinction due to habitat degradation and from pressures of the pet trade.

children.name: Abronia anzuetoi
children.description: The Anzuetoi arboreal alligator lizard (Abronia anzuetoi), also known commonly as Anzueto's arboreal alligator lizard, is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae. The species is endemic to Volcán de Agua in Guatemala.

children.name: Abronia leurolepis
children.description: Abronia leurolepis is an arboreal alligator lizard that is endemic to Mexico.

children.name: Abronia chiszari
children.description: Abronia chiszari, Chiszar's arboreal alligator lizard, is an endangered species of arboreal alligator lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Abronia martindelcampoi
children.commonName: Martín del Campo's Arboreal Alligator Lizard
children.description: Abronia martindelcampoi, also known commonly as Martín del Campo's arboreal alligator lizard and escorpión arborícola de Martín del Campo in Mexican Spanish, is an endangered species of lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Abronia ochoterenai
children.description: Abronia ochoterenai, also known commonly as Ochoterena's arboreal alligator lizard, the northern Chiapas arboreal alligator lizard, and escorpión arboricola de Ochoterena in Mexican Spanish, is a species of arboreal alligator lizard in the subfamily Gerrhonotinae of the family Anguidae.

children.name: Gerrhonotus
children.description: Alligator lizards of Texas, Mexico, and Central America; larger-bodied than Elgaria with prominent keeled scales and a distinct lateral fold. They inhabit rocky semi-arid terrain, canyon walls, and scrub.

children.name: Gerrhonotus liocephalus
children.description: Gerrhonotus liocephalus, also known commonly as the Texas alligator lizard, Wiegmann's alligator lizard, and la culebra con pata in Spanish, is a species of lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Gerrhonotus infernalis
children.description: The Texas alligator lizard (Gerrhonotus infernalis) is a species of lizard in the subfamily Gerrhonotinae of the family Anguidae.

children.name: Gerrhonotus ophiurus
children.description: Gerrhonotus ophiurus is a species of lizard of the Anguidae family.

children.name: Gerrhonotus parvus
children.description: Gerrhonotus parvus (common name: pygmy alligator lizard) is a species of lizard in the subfamily Gerrhonotinae.

children.name: Gerrhonotus lugoi
children.description: Gerrhonotus lugoi, also known commonly as Lugo's alligator lizard and la lagartija escorpion de Lugo in Mexican Spanish, is a species of lizard in the subfamily Gerrhonotinae of the family Anguidae.

children.name: Barisia
children.description: Montane alligator lizards of the Mexican highlands; viviparous, keeled-scaled lizards inhabiting pine-oak and fir forests above 1 500 m elevation across the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt and Sierra Madre.

children.name: Barisia imbricata
children.description: Barisia imbricata, also known commonly as the imbricate alligator lizard, the transvolcanic alligator lizard, and el escorpión de transvolcánico in Mexican Spanish, is a species of medium-sized lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Barisia rudicollis
children.description: The rough-necked alligator lizard (Barisia rudicollis) is a species of medium-sized lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Barisia jonesi
children.description: Barisia jonesi, also known commonly as the imbricate alligator lizard, Jones' imbricate alligator lizard, and el escorpión de Jones in Mexican Spanish, is a species of medium-sized lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Barisia levicollis
children.description: Barisia levicollis, also known commonly as the Chihuahuan alligator lizard and el escorpión de Chihuhua in Mexican Spanish, is a species of medium-sized lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Barisia herrerae
children.description: Herrera's alligator lizard (Barisia herrerae) is a species of medium-sized lizard in the family Anguidae.

children.name: Mesaspis
children.description: Cloud-forest alligator lizards of Central America and southern Mexico; viviparous, high-altitude specialists inhabiting oak-moss forests from Chiapas to Panama. They are among the highest-ranging lizards in Mesoamerica.

children.name: Mesaspis moreletii
children.description: Abronia moreletii, commonly known as Morelet's alligator lizard and escorpión de Morelet in Spanish, is a species of lizard in the subfamily Gerrhonotinae of the family Anguidae.

children.name: Mesaspis gadovii
children.description: From the highlands of Oaxaca and Chiapas, Mexico; named after the zoologist Hans Gadow, who studied Mexican reptiles. Inhabits cool, mossy cloud forest at elevations above 2 000 m. Its dark colouration and small size are adaptations to a cool, montane environment.

children.name: Mesaspis monticola
children.description: Distributed from Guatemala to Costa Rica; the most southerly-ranging Mesaspis. Inhabits cool montane forest and páramo-like grasslands above 2 000 m. Viviparous; litters are small (2–5 young), a common trait in high-altitude viviparous lizards.

children.name: Mesaspis unicolor
children.description: From Chiapas and adjacent Guatemala; distinguished by its relatively plain, unpatterned dorsum compared to other Mesaspis. Found in pine-oak cloud forest between 1 800 and 2 800 m. Little published field data exist on its ecology, though it is presumed viviparous.

children.name: Mesaspis viridiflava
children.description: Found in the highlands of Chiapas, Mexico; characterised by greenish-yellow lateral flank coloration in adults. Inhabits humid montane forest and rocky clearings. Named for its distinctive flank coloration, it is among the more visually identifiable Mesaspis.

children.name: Coloptychon
children.description: A monotypic genus of large Central American alligator lizard; the largest member of Gerrhonotinae, found in premontane and montane forest from Guatemala to western Panama.
